body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17: Loam issues no refresh tokens at all. `grep -n refresh src/server/oauth.ts`
returns nothing. The authorization-server document advertises
`grant_types_supported: ["authorization_code"]`, and Claude's own registration body asks for
`["authorization_code","refresh_token"]` — it wants one and the store has none.

WHAT IT COSTS. An access token expires and the connector stops working until Myk re-runs the whole
browser flow: sign in, read the consent page, approve. For a connector meant to be ambient — the
assistant that reads and writes his primary store all day — that is the difference between
infrastructure and a demo. Nothing is BROKEN today; the promise is just smaller than a connector needs.

THIS IS MYK'S MERGE AND MYK'S DECISION, because it changes what the system promises: a refresh token
is a credential that outlives the human's presence at the browser, and issuing one is a statement
about how long a connector may act without being re-asked.

DECISIONS BEFORE CODE:
D1 — LIFETIME. How long may a refresh token live, and does it expire at all? A grow-only store with a
  never-expiring refresh token has handed out a permanent key. Recommendation: a bounded lifetime with
  a stated number, plus revocation that binds at once (which already exists — `loam grant revoke`
  bumps the generation and every live token stops matching).
D2 — ROTATION. Does redeeming a refresh token issue a new one and retire the old (rotation), or reuse
  it? Recommendation: ROTATE, and treat a re-use of a retired refresh token as theft — refuse and
  revoke the whole grant. This is the standard defence and it is cheap here because the generation
  counter already exists.
D3 — WHAT IT CAN REFRESH INTO. Recommendation: exactly the scope originally consented to, never more.
  A refresh must not be a widening path.
D4 — WHERE IT LIVES AT REST. `oauth.json` holds clients, codes and grants today. A refresh token is a
  secret; decide whether it is stored hashed (so the file's disclosure is not a key) — recommendation:
  yes, hashed, the same posture credentials.json takes for passwords.

FROZEN RAIL COST, known up front: `test/server/oauth-token.test.ts` (T136) pins the token door and
`test/server/oauth-discovery.test.ts` (T133) pins `grant_types_supported`. Both will move. That is two
authorization pairs and therefore a PR before the PR — land the pairs, then the feature. Generate the
pairs from the diff and verify the gate answers EXEMPT against a synthetic base first.

RAILS:
1. A refresh grant issues a new access token that opens the MCP door, and the OLD access token stops
   opening it.
2. Rotation: the old refresh token is refused after use, and its re-use revokes the grant (assert the
   generation moved and a subsequent refresh fails).
3. The refreshed token's scope EQUALS the consented scope — assert equality, not membership, so a
   widening cannot pass.
4. `loam grant revoke` kills a refresh token at once, no restart, and the report says so.
5. The discovery document advertises `refresh_token` only once the door honours it — the anti-overclaim
   rail, comparing the advertised list to the grant types the token door actually accepts.
6. At rest: the refresh secret is not readable from oauth.json (hashed, per D4 if accepted).

PART OF THE CONNECTOR ARC, phase 2. The four phase-1 tickets (T176, T177, T178, T148) make the
connector work at all; this one makes it stay working.
title: A connector's grant cannot be refreshed, so every expiry costs the operator a browser round trip
